entry.title: New York Times and Other Publishers Sue Brave Software Over Content Scraping
entry.content:
Links: techcrunch.com

The New York Times, alongside other news publishers including the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, has filed dual lawsuits in Manhattan federal court against Brave Software. The complaints allege that the privacy-focused browser company unlawfully scraped tens of billions of copyrighted webpages using an unblockable crawler and distributed the content to artificial intelligence firms such as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.

The lawsuits also take aim at specific features within the Brave browser, claiming the software helps users bypass paywalls while blocking publisher advertisements in favor of its own. The publishers are seeking both an injunction and financial damages against the 11-year-old browser company, which has not yet responded to requests for comment.

entry.title: Putin Orders Private Data Centers in Russia to Reserve 10% Capacity for State IT
entry.content:
Links: reuters.com | hacker news

Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree requiring owners of non-state data centers to reserve 10% of their space and capacity to support the country's IT infrastructure and state information resources. The measure follows recent Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian facilities and growing concerns over the security of domestic digital networks.

Under the directive, commercial data center operators must set aside the required capacity to ensure critical online resources remain operational in the event of disruptions or emergencies. The decision builds on recent recommendations from Russia's Ministry of Digital Development aimed at fortifying digital infrastructure against aerial threats.

entry.title: Scott Alexander Publishes Against SURA Essay on LessWrong
entry.content:
Links: lesswrong.com

Blogger Scott Alexander published an essay on LessWrong examining the rising popularity of what he terms "SURA"—Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness—within AI safety debates. He argues that safety-focused AI labs should not abandon the ongoing AI race, contending that a unilateral pause would hand leadership to organizations that do not prioritize alignment and eliminate strategic leverage against competitors like China.

The essay has sparked intra-community debate over AI pause movements, safety strategies, and how ethical labs should navigate competitive pressures. Critics and commentators have engaged with the arguments surrounding whether unilateral cessation or continuing participation is more effective for ensuring safe AI development.

entry.title: Elon Musk Spends Record $474 Million on 2026 Midterm Elections
entry.content:
Links: nytimes.com

Elon Musk has contributed $474 million to political groups during the 2026 midterm election cycle, setting a record for the most money ever spent by a non-candidate single donor in a single election cycle. His financial outlay includes $216 million to his own super PAC, America PAC, $168 million to the Senate Leadership Fund largely supporting the Republican nominee in Texas, and tens of millions more directed toward House committees and state-level efforts.

The massive spending push is designed to help Republicans retain control of Congress as Musk confronts potential Democratic scrutiny over his government efficiency initiatives, federal contracts, and foreign policy stances. His total surpasses all previous individual non-candidate donors, trailing only the self-funded presidential campaign spending of Michael Bloomberg in 2020.

entry.title: Hundreds of AI Apps on Apple and Google App Stores Hid Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
entry.content:
Links: wired.com

An investigation by WIRED and security researchers has uncovered a network of more than 400 applications and domains disguised as mundane tools, such as pet portrait generators and workout apps, that secretly feature sexually abusive deepfake tools. These applications bypassed review processes on Apple’s App Store and Google’s Play Store by dynamically loading hidden web interfaces that generate explicit images and videos from uploaded user photos.

The network, linked to Chinese developers and a Hong Kong entity named KeLing Technology Limited, was heavily promoted through tens of thousands of deceptive video ads on Meta platforms like Facebook and Instagram. Although tech companies have since removed many of the associated apps and banned related ad accounts, the operation highlights ongoing vulnerabilities in app store vetting and ad moderation systems that allow harmful deepfake features to evade detection.

entry.title: Brazilian Labor Court Fines Lawyers for Prompt Injection in Court Filing
entry.content:
Links: jetstream.security | hacker news

A Brazilian labor court fined two lawyers after discovering a hidden prompt-injection command embedded within a court filing to manipulate the judiciary's artificial intelligence review system. Rendered in white font on a white background, the concealed instruction directed the Galileu AI tool to process the petition superficially and avoid challenging submitted documents.

The court sanctioned the representing law firms 10 percent of the claim's value for violating procedural good-faith duties and undermining institutional respect under the Brazilian Civil Procedure Code. As legal systems increasingly adopt automated tools for document processing, this ruling underscores the emerging security challenges surrounding machine-readable content in judicial proceedings.

entry.title: Federal Judge Allows NAACP Clean Air Act Lawsuit Against xAI to Proceed
entry.content:
Links: techcrunch.com | earthjustice.org

A federal judge has denied a motion by xAI to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit brought by the NAACP and the Southern Environmental Law Center. The litigation accuses the AI company of operating dozens of gas combustion turbines without required preconstruction or operating permits to power its Colossus data center near Memphis.

xAI had argued that the lawsuit should be thrown out because the turbines qualify as mobile sources and are thus exempt from permits, while also challenging the plaintiffs' standing. Judge Debra M. Brown rejected these arguments, affirming that the plaintiffs have statutory standing and that citizen suits do not violate the Constitution. The case moves forward amid growing public scrutiny and regulatory pushback against the environmental impact of large data centers.

entry.title: Congressional Lawmakers Introduce Resolution Opposing AI Bubble Bailout for Big Tech
entry.content:
Links: progressives.house.gov | hacker news

Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar and House Financial Services Committee Ranking Member Maxine Waters, alongside several Democratic lawmakers, introduced a resolution warning of severe economic risks posed by an artificial intelligence asset bubble. The measure formally opposes federal bailouts for insolvent A.I. corporations or their executives, demanding instead that corporate leaders face civil and criminal accountability if their reckless investments collapse.

Drawing parallels to the 2008 financial crisis, the resolution urges the federal government to bypass corporate rescues and direct any emergency intervention toward protecting workers, retirees, and low-income communities through job creation, unemployment insurance, and housing assistance. The initiative is backed by numerous labor unions and economic advocacy groups, including the American Federation of Teachers, Americans for Financial Reform, and the Center for Economic and Policy Research.

entry.title: Melanie Kat Examines Public Data Exposure on AT Protocol Personal Data Servers
entry.content:
Links: melaniekat.com | lobsters

Developer and researcher Melanie Kat examines how data generated by applications built on the AT Protocol—such as feed subscriptions, chat logs, and third-party app usage—is stored openly on personal data servers (PDS). By inspecting public relays and indexing tools, the investigation reveals that user information, including private RSS subscriptions, paywalled content feeds, and real-time chat messages, can be accessed without authentication.

The findings highlight potential privacy risks for users who may not realize that third-party applications built on decentralized networks publish their activity streams publicly. While transparency is foundational to the protocol's architecture, the ease of aggregating and searching this data raises concerns about whether everyday users fully understand the visibility of their digital footprints.
